What you’re seeing

β = θ − θE² / θ   ·   θE ∝ √M

Gravitational lensing. The black hole curves spacetime, and light follows that curved geometry. This simplified thin-lens equation maps an observed image angle (θ) to a source angle (β). The model uses it to warp the background star field; it is an educational approximation, not a full general-relativistic ray trace.

Einstein ring and multiple images. When a source lies almost directly behind the lens, light can reach the observer along many directions, producing a near-ring. Moving the source off-axis breaks the ring into brighter arcs or multiple images.

Event horizon vs photon sphere. The dark central shadow represents the region from which light cannot escape. The photon sphere is outside the event horizon, where light can orbit temporarily in the idealised Schwarzschild case. Neither is drawn to a universal scale here.

Black holes don’t “suck everything in”. Far away, their gravity behaves like that of any object with the same mass. An object on a stable orbit can keep orbiting; dramatic capture requires a trajectory that brings it sufficiently close or removes enough orbital energy.

Educational note: the display exaggerates the near-hole features for visibility. Real lensing depends on source and observer distances, black-hole spin, accretion physics and the full relativistic spacetime geometry.
